reverse_outline.summary: Three takeaways: platform as many systems keeping promises, business model shapes systems, map jobs and owners before choosing a platform
One order spawns work across many systems that back the storefront's promises
Part I's thesis: the platform is all promise-keeping systems, and failures are broken handoffs
Introducing the fictional Kestrel & Pine example and its tangled systems + its Waypoint program starting with ownership decisions
Roadmap of the five questions Part I answers in sequence
Chapter preview: tracing one order end to end and why a single status misleads
Chapter preview: business model determines systems + growth through four scale stages
Chapter preview: capability map revealing gaps and duplicate writers
Chapter preview: naming one owning record per fact, separating records from copies
Chapter preview: platform categories shift integration work; Kestrel & Pine keeps its shop and fills gaps
Problems are ownership gaps, not product gaps + advice on reading order

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
The intro reader named all five chapters in order (order journey; selling models; capability map; one record per fact; platforms the market sells), matching the expected answer.
Every outline summary matches the controlling idea of its aligned spec paragraph (p01-p10); the callout has no spec paragraph by design.

results.quote: As a merchant grows, that shape changes: it adds channels, locations, countries and brands. The book calls these steps four scale stages, from Starting (one online shop) to Group (several brands).
results.finding: The outliner read the scale stages as a second idea beside 'the shape of the business decides the systems'. The draft never says the stages are defined by shape rather than revenue or that they change the systems needed (the spec's 'not by passing a revenue threshold'), so the stages read as a separate topic rather than the same idea over time.
Introduction ¶1-¶4 set up the part claim and roadmap; the five chapter paragraphs trace to P1-1..P1-5 in turn; the closing restates the claim through Kestrel & Pine.

Figures 1-3 each carry a caption stating what they show; the Kestrel & Pine numbers are tied to 'four places' and 'six writers'; the two rebuilds are explained by 'adds what is missing' and the closing's 'no product fixes that'.

All declared transitions are carried: 'those promises' (elaboration), 'The example is' (example), 'Part I asks Kestrel & Pine' (sequence), 'keeps those steps but' (contrast), 'then maps' (sequence), 'which the map alone cannot settle' (contrast), 'comes last, once jobs are mapped' (sequence), and the closing's summary of the company's problems (conclusion_summary).

Each does_not_know term is glossed where it appears: shop platform ('that runs the webshop'), writers ('systems or people'), capabilities ('jobs'), records and copies, scale stages (named with Starting/Group), platform categories (who hosts, upgrades, integrates). Eva is not named.

results.quote: The book calls these steps four scale stages, from Starting (one online shop) to Group (several brands).
results.finding: flow-A: 'I had to re-read this... at first I read "these steps" as the order steps'. 'Steps' names the thirteen order steps one sentence earlier ('keeps those steps') and then the growth stages.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B: item 2, same sentence ('Here I lost the thread... The same word now names a different thing')

results.quote: another, shown at once as delivered by the shop, in picking by the warehouse and not invoiced by finance, shows why one status word cannot explain everything.
results.finding: flow-A: 'I had to re-read this to parse it. "Shown at once as" is compressed.' The long inserted clause hides that one order carries three conflicting statuses at the same moment.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B: item 1, same sentence ('I had to read this twice')

results.quote: Kestrel & Pine's problems are unowned facts at the handoffs where the shopper's order breaks; no product fixes that.
results.finding: flow-A: 'I read it twice to connect "unowned facts"... with "handoffs"... and "no product"'. The sentence packs three chapters' ideas into one clause, and 'no product fixes that' sits oddly right after the company 'adds what is missing'.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B: item 6, same sentence ('dense... I had to pause')

results.finding: The introduction opens on a concrete example (one order and the systems behind it), then states the claim; no weak pattern.
The closing is a short synthesis drawn from the example plus reading advice; no new subtopic, no 'in conclusion' opener, not a bare restatement of the thesis.
'Kestrel & Pine's problems are unowned facts at the handoffs...; no product fixes that' synthesizes the chapters and answers the so-what (look at the handoffs and ownership before buying a product).
'the handoffs where the shopper's order breaks' returns to the opening shopper's order, and the advice starts with the order's journey.

The reader chose boundaries-and-systems-of-record for the stock mismatch (record vs copies, six writers) and commerce-platform-landscape for the replacement (who hosts, upgrades and integrates; two rebuilds), matching the expected answer.

The reader gave all three expected reasons: the order's journey is the concrete case and supplies the steps later chapters build on; each answer is the next question's vocabulary; the landscape comes last once jobs are mapped and owners named.
